title: Construct the Lexicographically Largest Valid Sequence
statement:
Given an integer `n`, build an array of length `2n - 1` from the values `1` to `n` where:

- the value `1` appears exactly once;
- every value `v` from `2` to `n` appears exactly twice, and its two copies sit exactly `v` positions apart (at indices `i` and `j` with `|j - i| = v`).

Several arrays may follow these rules. Return the lexicographically largest one: comparing two candidates at the first index where they differ, the larger one holds the bigger value there. A valid array always exists for the allowed `n`.
notes:
## Intuition

Listing every valid arrangement and keeping the largest works only for tiny `n`. Lexicographic order rewards the front of the array most, so fill the cells from left to right and give each empty cell the largest value that can still be completed. With values tried from `n` down to `1`, the first full arrangement backtracking reaches is already the answer, and the search can stop there.

## Approach

1. Make `result` of length `size = 2n - 1` filled with `0` (empty), and a `used` flag per value.
2. `place(index)` returns `true` once `index` reaches `size`: every cell is filled.
3. If the cell already holds a value (it was the second copy of an earlier value), move on to `index + 1`.
4. Otherwise try each unused `value` from `n` down to `1`. Its second copy goes to `partner = index + value`; the value `1` has no second copy, so its `partner` is `index` itself.
5. Skip the value if `partner` is past the end or already filled. Else write both cells, mark it used and recurse; on success return `true`, otherwise erase both cells and try the next value.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 3`, so `size = 5`. At index 0 the value 3 fits with its partner at 3: `[3,0,0,3,0]`. At index 1, 3 is used and 2 would need cell 3, which is taken, so 1 goes there: `[3,1,0,3,0]`. At index 2 the value 2 fits with its partner at 4: `[3,1,2,3,2]`. Indices 3 and 4 are already filled, index 5 equals `size`, and the answer is `[3,1,2,3,2]`.

## Complexity

- Time: exponential in the worst case, since each empty cell may try up to `n` values; trying large values first finds a solution almost at once for every `n <= 20`.
- Space: O(n) for `result`, `used` and the recursion, which is at most `2n - 1` deep.

## Pitfalls

- The value `1` fills a single cell; treating it like the others would demand a second copy.
- A filled cell must be skipped, not overwritten: it holds the partner of an earlier value.
- When undoing a choice, clear both cells and the `used` flag.
- Stop at the first complete arrangement; searching on would only find smaller ones.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `size` | length of the answer, `2n - 1` |
| `result` | the arrangement being built, `0` for an empty cell |
| `used` | `used[v]` is true when `v` is already placed |
| `index` | the cell being filled |
| `value` | the candidate value for that cell |
| `partner` | the cell for the second copy of `value` |

narration.2: The answer holds 1 once and every other value twice, so it has 2n - 1 cells.
narration.3: Every cell starts empty, marked by 0.
narration.4: used[v] records whether value v is already in the array.
narration.6: place(index) tries to complete the array from this cell onward and reports success.
narration.7: Past the last cell means every cell is filled: a valid arrangement.
narration.10: This cell already holds the second copy of an earlier value...
narration.11: ...so just continue with the next cell.
narration.13: Try values from largest to smallest so the first success is the lexicographically largest.
narration.14: A value already placed cannot be used again.
narration.17: The second copy goes value cells to the right; 1 has no second copy and stays in this cell.
narration.18: The second copy must land inside the array on an empty cell.
narration.21: Commit to this value: mark it used...
narration.24: Try to fill the remaining cells with this choice in place.
narration.25: It worked, so pass the success back up without trying smaller values.
narration.27: It failed: undo the choice so the next value can be tried.
narration.32: No value fits here, so the caller must change an earlier choice.
narration.35: Start filling from the first cell.
narration.36: result now holds the largest valid arrangement.
